article_title: Journeys
citation: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt Journeys: Evidence Review. (2017). https://www.hmhco.com/programs/journeys
title: Whole-group introduction followed by small-group homogeneous practice of the same skills
description: The Journeys program organizes daily literacy instruction in two tiers: whole group activities introduce a "big idea" and "essential question" for the day, a teacher read-aloud, and vocabulary, phonics, comprehension, and fluency activities. Small group activities then "follow up these same skills in small, homogeneous groups," so all students meet the same content with differentiated group support.
requirements: Grade-level classroom teacher guiding whole-group, small-group, and independent sessions
constraints: Evaluated only in grades K-2
examples: Small group activities follow up the same skills introduced in whole group instruction in small, homogeneous groups.
key_sources: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt Journeys: Evidence Review. (2017). https://www.hmhco.com/programs/journeys

article_title: Predicting time to reclassification for English learners: A joint modeling approach
citation: Tyler Matta, James Soland. (2018). Predicting time to reclassification for English learners: A joint modeling approach. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics. https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998618791259
title: Model English proficiency development jointly with reclassification timing when predicting EL outcomes
description: Because the joint model outperformed the conventional approach, the article supports designing EL policy analytics that estimate proficiency growth and reclassification timing together rather than separately. The SREM treats "student-specific random effects as latent covariates in the time to reclassification model," yielding more accurate predictions of the grade of reclassification.
requirements: Access to longitudinal English proficiency measures linked to reclassification records
constraints: Evidence comes from one large Arizona school district
target_learning_goals: Accurate prediction of reclassification to fluent English proficient status
examples: The authors fit the SREM to Arizona district data and compared its prediction accuracy (93%) with a conventional discrete-time hazard model (85%).
key_sources: Tyler Matta, James Soland. (2018). Predicting time to reclassification for English learners: A joint modeling approach. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics. https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998618791259

article_title: AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era
citation: Eliana Khoury & Xiaoyan Ma. (2026). AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era. Journal of Teaching and Learning, 20(4). https://doi.org/10.22329/jtl.v20i4.11850
title: Joyful assessment: a rigorous, learner-centered framework for assessment design in the GenAI era
description: The paper proposes joyful assessment as "a rigorous and learner-centered framework for assessment design in the GenAI era", synthesizing scholarship on assessment validity, relational and compassionate assessment, third space theory, and AI agents. Joyful assessment is defined as "assessment that is safe, emotionally responsive, empowering, and supportive of student agency".
requirements: Assessment must be designed to be safe, emotionally responsive, empowering, and supportive of student agency rather than organized primarily around misconduct prevention or AI detection.
constraints: The framework is proposed in a conceptual paper; the authors conclude by identifying future research directions related to responsible design, learner experience, equity, validity, and relational assessment practice.
examples: The paper states that it "demonstrates these ideas through a practical example".
key_sources: Eliana Khoury & Xiaoyan Ma. (2026). AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era. Journal of Teaching and Learning, 20(4). https://doi.org/10.22329/jtl.v20i4.11850

article_title: Understanding student perspectives on generative AI chatbots: a human-centred mixed-methods study in higher education
citation: Stephen Colbran, Meena Jha and Caitlin Schiavone. (2026). Understanding student perspectives on generative AI chatbots: a human-centred mixed-methods study in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00605-w
title: Jordan Chatbot: a unit-specific GPT-4o pedagogical support agent grounded in constructivist and socio-cultural learning theory
description: The Jordan Chatbot is a human-centred, pedagogical support agent built on the GPT-4o large language model and deployed as a unit-specific conversational agent within the LMS. The article states it "integrates three core components: (1) system instructions defining the chatbot's identity, personality, inclusions, and exclusions; (2) a curated knowledge base containing disciplinary and institutional materials; and (3) an embedded interface within the LMS". Its design draws on situated learning theory and Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, positioning the chatbot as a mediating tool that extends but does not replace teacher guidance, and supports self-regulated learning through immediate personalised feedback.
requirements: A curated knowledge base of unit learning materials and institutional resources to ground responses and reduce inaccurate outputs
System prompts defining the pedagogical role, behavioural boundaries and response limitations, including restrictions on answering assessment-related questions
Deployment within the LMS by developers rather than academic staff to ensure consistency and standards
constraints: Configured not to answer assessment-related questions
Selected over general-purpose chatbots to comply with institutional privacy and governance requirements
target_learners: Undergraduate business and law students at a regional Australian university
target_learning_goals: Navigating unit content, assessment requirements and institutional resources
Clarifying difficult disciplinary concepts and supporting self-directed study
examples: Deployed across nine undergraduate business and law units in Term 1, 2025, with curated unit materials and continual monitoring of edge cases by altering system instructions or the knowledge base
key_sources: Stephen Colbran, Meena Jha and Caitlin Schiavone. (2026). Understanding student perspectives on generative AI chatbots: a human-centred mixed-methods study in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00605-w

article_title: Probing AI-Generated Physics Solutions and Preparing Students to Critique Them
citation: Nikhil Sanjay Borse, Amir Bralin, Sean Savage, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). Probing AI-generated physics solutions and preparing students to critique them. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12533
title: Jonassen-informed prompt-variation framework with MAPS-based evaluation for probing LRM physics reasoning
description: The article adapts Jonassen's problem-classification framework to generative-AI problem solving along two dimensions: "prompt-specificity, or how much information is explicitly given versus left for the model to infer, and modality, or whether the problem is presented through text alone or with visual representations". Combined with the MAPS rubric, which scores useful descriptions, physics approach, specific application, mathematical procedures, and logical progression, this provides "a structured way to probe these dimensions of LRM reasoning" beyond final-answer accuracy.
requirements: Requires a reasoning-capable LRM accessible via API and a problem family amenable to systematic removal of prompt details and text-visual variation
constraints: The study used one model, o4-mini, and one rotational-mechanics problem family, so findings may not generalize across models, topics, or domains, though the authors state the method remains transferable
target_learning_goals: critically evaluating AI-generated physics solutions with disciplinary criteria
examples: Three representative prompt variants of a rotating-bowl rolling-sphere problem were each submitted five times and scored with the MAPS rubric (Table I).
key_sources: Nikhil Sanjay Borse, Amir Bralin, Sean Savage, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). Probing AI-generated physics solutions and preparing students to critique them. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12533

article_title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
citation: Sidney Shapiro and Joshua Lindemann. (2026). On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02510
title: Treat model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision when building a campus AI tutor
description: The article argues that a tutoring system's quality cannot be improved by swapping one component in isolation: latency, memory, retrieval, and product surfaces interact. As the abstract concludes, "The results support treating model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision." The bake-off held the retrieval stack fixed to make generator comparisons interpretable, and a separate experiment changed model and response contract together so its gains could not be attributed to scale alone.
requirements: Keep the serving retrieval stack fixed during model comparisons so failures are traceable
Promotion requires clearing a classroom speed gate plus a demonstrated quality improvement
constraints: The authors state they do not claim that 8B is universally optimal, and no controlled learning-outcome comparison is reported
target_learning_goals: grounded explanations of assigned course material
examples: The project retained the 8B production model despite sufficient memory to trial larger candidates, because no replacement demonstrated the required combination of quality, continuity, integration, and operational readiness
key_sources: Sidney Shapiro and Joshua Lindemann. (2026). On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02510

article_title: Through the WordStream Glass: Revisiting Quantitative Encoding for Qualitative Learning Analytics
citation: Huyen N. Nguyen, Kathleen A. Bowe, Minh-Huyen Nguyen, Kit Thompson, Caleb M. Trujillo. (2026). Through the WordStream Glass: Revisiting Quantitative Encoding for Qualitative Learning Analytics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18692
title: Journal Data Dashboard: multi-panel WordStream tool linking aggregate trends to verbatim student responses
description: The Journal Data Dashboard is a domain-specific, multi-panel tool that links a WordStream visualization to the weekly prompts students answered and to the full text of their responses, so that "selecting a word retrieves the responses that contain it, supporting movement from the aggregate view to individual student writing." It is built around a fixed assessment corpus and supports insight extraction. In this study it served as a probe into the insight-extraction stage of an analytical workflow.
requirements: A fixed assessment corpus with verbatim student responses to which the visualization can link
constraints: Domain-specific: limited, preset customization and no user-uploaded data
target_learning_goals: Tracking the temporal evolution of student language in written reflections and formative assessments
examples: Ten instructor-researchers explored the Dashboard on 62 students' weekly written reflections from a data visualization course
key_sources: Huyen N. Nguyen, Kathleen A. Bowe, Minh-Huyen Nguyen, Kit Thompson, Caleb M. Trujillo. (2026). Through the WordStream Glass: Revisiting Quantitative Encoding for Qualitative Learning Analytics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18692

article_title: Reconsidering the Use of Oral Exams and Assessments: An Old Way to Move Into a New Future
citation: Fenton, A. (2025). Reconsidering the Use of Oral Exams and Assessments: An Old Way to Move Into a New Future. Educational Researcher, 54(7), 430-436. https://doi.org/10.3102/0013189X251333638
title: Joughin's six-dimension taxonomy characterizes oral assessments
description: The article presents a taxonomy of oral assessments along six dimensions: primary content type, interaction, authenticity, structure, examiners, and orality. It also distinguishes two qualities oral assessments can measure: "the student's oral skills in communication, and the second is the command of the content as demonstrated through the oral medium." The article uses this taxonomy to show oral assessments vary widely in form, from presentation to dialogue, and that educators' design choices along these dimensions determine what the assessment measures.
requirements: Educators must decide how exactly to structure the assessment along the dimensions, since both strict exam and interactive-oral definitions are valid depending on structure
examples: The article lists the six dimensions as primary content type, interaction, authenticity, structure, examiners, and orality, citing Joughin (1998)
key_sources: Fenton, A. (2025). Reconsidering the Use of Oral Exams and Assessments: An Old Way to Move Into a New Future. Educational Researcher, 54(7), 430-436. https://doi.org/10.3102/0013189X251333638

article_title: Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus
citation: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283
title: Attentional regulation account: joint attentional focus explains the relationship between maternal directives and vocabulary development
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which the effect of maternal directives on vocabulary depends on whether the directive respects the child's current focus of attention. Because prescriptives "are most often used to redirect a child's attention to a different object or activity", the authors hypothesize that "attentional regulation underlies this negative relationship" between directiveness and vocabulary growth. Directives delivered within a joint focus of attention are predicted to be beneficial, while attention-changing directives are not.
requirements: Coding of maternal directives by their relation to the child's focus of attention (LEADING vs FOLLOWING), as the study operationalized the account
constraints: The account is tested with a small correlational sample of twelve mother-child dyads, so causal direction is not established in the available text
examples: The study videotaped twelve mothers interacting with children aged 1;1 and coded 100 maternal utterances each for pragmatic intent, distinguishing LEADING from FOLLOWING prescriptives
key_sources: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283

article_title: Reigniting CSCL flash themes
citation: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse. (2013). Reigniting CSCL flash themes. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:369–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9185-0
title: Joint attention as foundational to collaborative interaction, investigable through eye-tracking support of gaze coordination
description: The editors present joint attention as foundational to collaborative interaction and human sociality: from infancy on, people learn to use different forms and media of joint attention to make intersubjective sense, and communication requires a coordinated orientation to a shared object understood as shared. For two people to solve a problem together, they must take the problem as the same problem and see the object as the same object. The issue's eye-tracking study investigates this by letting students see where their partners' eyes are gazing at a like screen, so that staring in a similar direction can be elaborated into a sense of making shared meaning.
requirements: Objective data on gaze must be tied to intersubjective meaning making if gaze is to be used as an indicator of joint attention
target_learners: dyads of students in CSCL settings
examples: In the experimental condition of the Schneider and Pea study, students could see where the eyes of their partners were gazing at a computer screen like their own screen, as an information source in addition to their audio connection.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse. (2013). Reigniting CSCL flash themes. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:369–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9185-0

article_title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8
title: Run a research journal as a mechanism of community-based collaborative learning that pairs publication with detailed anonymous critique and revision.
description: The editorial proposes that a journal serving a research field can function simultaneously as a formal publication channel and as peer-guided learning: virtually all published papers went through "extensive critique and revision," and even rejected papers received detailed reviews. The reviewers and Editorial Board "contributed significantly to guiding the major revisions through which all accepted papers passed," so the community establishes the journal's content and tone. This makes the review process itself a vehicle for mutual assistance and learning within the community.
requirements: An engaged Editorial Board and additional reviewers willing to provide deep, detailed constructive feedback on submissions, including papers that are not ultimately published.
constraints: Journal interaction is anonymous, which the authors say allows critique that is more frank and detailed than at conferences, but it lacks the informality and direct interaction of meetings and conferences.
target_learners: Research authors submitting papers to the CSCL community
target_learning_goals: Improving research writing, argumentation, and understanding of what is needed for future publication
examples: During ijCSCL's first year, virtually all published papers passed through extensive critique and revision, and the many unpublished papers each received several detailed reviews.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8

article_title: A New Statistical Book for Research Workers.
citation: H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeduropsych
title: Jones' A First Course in Statistics (1921), a two-part statistics textbook for education and psychology research workers
description: The reviewed artifact is Jones' textbook 'A First Course in Statistics' (G. Bell & Sons, London, 1921, pp. IX + 286). Part I, using economic and biological illustrations, covers "variables and frequency distribution; classification and tabulation of materials; averages, dispersion, graphs and correlation." Part II gives students "access to a treatment of probability, sampling, curve fitting and type distribution curves."
requirements: Intended for research students in psychology and education who need mathematical foundations beyond existing American measurement books
constraints: The reviewer notes partial correlation is not discussed, so students must still consult Yule's detailed original publication
target_learners: Research students in psychology and education
target_learning_goals: Statistical treatment of data: frequency distributions, averages, dispersion, correlation, probability, sampling, curve fitting
examples: The reviewer cites Part I's use of economic and biological illustrations and Part II's treatment of probability, sampling, curve fitting and type distribution curves
key_sources: H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeduropsych

article_title: Recent publications in history [Four articles and two books].
citation: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Johnson's conception of history teaching: making the social world intelligible as the permanent aim
description: Johnson's book, which the reviewer calls the most recent, most incisive and most illuminating study of history teaching yet to appear, contrasts the simple narrative and moralist-didactic types of historical account with the modern scientific conception that strives for objective interpretation of social conditions. Of all proposed aims, the reviewer reports Johnson holds "the only really permanent aim is to under- stand the world in which we live,—to make the social world intelligible," so history is studied for its own sake rather than for disciplinary or moral advantage. Johnson's task for the teacher is making the past real, employing all imaginable aids and allowing pupils' self-activity.
requirements: History work confined to interpreting the past; Johnson recommends leaving imaginative re-creation of historic characters to literature and treating today's governmental organizations as contemporary rather than historical phenomena
constraints: Johnson expresses doubt that correlation schemes with geography, literature and government may be detrimental to history itself and disorganizing for other subjects
target_learning_goals: Understanding the present social world through acquaintance with the life of the past
examples: The book's first five chapters survey the history of the teaching of history, and chapters four and five survey history's curricular place from the sixteenth century onward, with reference to France, Germany and the United States
key_sources: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

article_title: Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning
citation: Zheng Zheng & Jun Wang. (2024). Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00280-4
title: Joint statistical learning complementary SRTT hyperscanning paradigm with OSF data release
description: A modified serial reaction time task in which a fixed 12-location stimulus sequence is randomly divided and assigned to each co-actor for response. The experiment comprised eight blocks: Blocks 1 to 6 and 8 were "constructed from a ﬁxed sequence of locations, while the seventh block was constructed from an interference sequence". Dyads were assigned to a joint context (both respond to pre-assigned colours) or a baseline context (actor plus passive observer), with concurrent dual-EEG recording at 512 Hz. All behaviour and EEG data, and in-house scripts, are deposited on the Open Science Framework.
requirements: Dual-EEG recording system with synchronized amplifiers
Paired participants randomly assigned to joint or baseline context
constraints: Interference and main sequence assignment counterbalanced across dyads; only female participants recruited
target_learning_goals: implicit statistical learning of fixed stimulus sequences in joint and individual contexts
examples: Data and scripts available at the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/wdctr/)
key_sources: Zheng Zheng & Jun Wang. (2024). Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00280-4

article_title: Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making
citation: Cochrane, A., Sims, C. R., Bejjanki, V. R., Green, C. S., & Bavelier, D. (2023). Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making. npj Science of Learning 8:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00168-9
title: Model learning with joint RT-and-accuracy diffusion models at the trial level rather than accuracy-only aggregated analyses
description: The article recommends analyzing learning with by-trial evidence-accumulation models fit to the joint distributions of response time and accuracy, rather than aggregating across sessions or relying on accuracy alone. It argues that "using only impoverished discrete-choice behavioral data could prevent or bias possible inferences regarding learning trajectories". The approach provides a clear justification for using the diffusion model's drift rate parameter as an index of perceptual learning as a function of each training trial.
requirements: Access to trial-level RT and accuracy data and Bayesian estimation tools such as brms/Stan; extensive computational resources, as the article notes at least several weeks of computer time per model
constraints: The article notes the models tested represent only a small portion of possible models of change, and interpretability of the response boundary parameter is more complex due to within-day and between-day dynamics
target_learners: adult learners in perceptual and cognitive training contexts
target_learning_goals: accurate inference about learning trajectories and underlying decision processes
examples: Fitting six candidate DDM parameterizations by trial across four days of dot-motion training, with the continuous DR flexible RB model winning the comparison
key_sources: Cochrane, A., Sims, C. R., Bejjanki, V. R., Green, C. S., & Bavelier, D. (2023). Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making. npj Science of Learning 8:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00168-9

article_title: Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies
citation: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z
title: Joint display analysis as an iterative process for identifying connections between qualitative and quantitative constructs and generating meta-inferences
description: The article defines joint display analysis, following Fetters and Guetterman (2021), as "an iterative process in which researchers use the joint display structure to identify connections between qualitative and quantitative constructs and generate meta-inferences" based on the fit of the two data types. This allows researchers to acquire new insights beyond those provided by each component individually. The article positions this as a tool for the "cognitive process of merging, comparing, relating, and linking qualitative and quantitative data or results" during study execution, supporting integration and inferential transparency.
requirements: Requires rigorous intra-method analysis of both strands as a first step before mixed analysis begins.
constraints: The article notes that meaningful integration of qualitative and quantitative data remains elusive and needs further development, citing Guetterman et al. (2015).
target_learning_goals: Conducting rigorous mixed methods integration in EdTech research
key_sources: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z

article_title: Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies
citation: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z
title: Assess joint display effectiveness using organizational intent, analytic intent, and effectiveness of the visual presentation
description: Following Haynes-Brown and Fetters (2021), the article states that "joint display effectiveness can be assessed on three criteria, namely, organizational intent, analytic intent, and the effectiveness of the visual presentation". In the illustrative study, organizational intent was to depict the ecological and integrated nature of learner experiences, analytic intent was to examine interconnections by evaluating the extent to which quantitative data supported qualitative findings, and effectiveness was evaluated by aiming for a display that was self-explanatory and avoided unnecessary complexity.
requirements: Requires iterative design review across publishing stages to improve organizational and analytical intent.
target_learning_goals: Designing and evaluating visual joint displays for mixed methods integration
examples: The authors piloted the meta-joint display in research seminars and conferences to infer whether the display was appealing and easily understood.
key_sources: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem-Solving Ability and Self-Confidence of High School Students through Contextual Learning Model
citation: Surya, E., Putri, F.A., & Mukhtar. (2017). Improving Mathematical Problem-Solving Ability and Self-Confidence of High School Students through Contextual Learning Model. Journal on Mathematics Education, 8(1), 85-94. https://jme.ejournal.ums.ac.id/index.php/jme
title: Johnson's eight components of contextual learning
description: The article enumerates eight components that Johnson (2007) says make up contextual learning: making meaningful linkages, independent learning, doing meaningful work, collaboration, thinking critically and creatively, helping people to grow and develop, achieving a high standard, and using authentic assessment. These components characterize how the contextual learning model operationalizes situated, student-centered mathematics instruction in the study.
requirements: Instruction should situate problem-solving in physical, intellectual, and social contexts the article calls relevant
target_learners: grade VIII junior high school mathematics students
examples: The experimental class's contextual lessons were the article's instantiation of these components against expository delivery of material
key_sources: Surya, E., Putri, F.A., & Mukhtar. (2017). Improving Mathematical Problem-Solving Ability and Self-Confidence of High School Students through Contextual Learning Model. Journal on Mathematics Education, 8(1), 85-94. https://jme.ejournal.ums.ac.id/index.php/jme

article_title: Promoting Social and Emotional Competencies in Elementary School
citation: Stephanie M. Jones, Sophie P. Barnes, Rebecca Bailey, and Emily J. Doolittle. (2017). Promoting Social and Emotional Competencies in Elementary School. The Future of Children, Vol. 27, No. 1, Spring 2017. https://www.futureofchildren.org
title: Jones three-domain framework organizing elementary SEL skills into cognitive regulation, emotional processes, and social/interpersonal skills
description: The article uses an organizing framework, developed by coauthor Stephanie Jones, that categorizes social and emotional skills and behaviors for the elementary years. As the article states, it "categorizes social and emotional skills and behaviors into three primary groups: cognitive regulation, emotional processes, and social/interpersonal skills." Cognitive regulation comprises basic cognitive skills for directing behavior toward goals, closely related to executive function (attention, inhibition, working memory). Emotional processes help children recognize, express, and regulate emotions and understand others' emotional perspectives. Social/interpersonal skills build on emotional knowledge and help children interpret others' behavior and navigate social situations. The framework is based on a review of developmental and prevention science and a scan of major SEL frameworks and curricular approaches, and it excludes attitudinal constructs such as character and mindsets.
requirements: Based on a review of research in developmental and prevention science and a scan of major defining frameworks and curricular approaches for SEL
constraints: Does not include attitudinal constructs such as character and mindsets, which are increasingly incorporated in other organizing frameworks largely with middle and high school students
target_learners: Children in middle childhood, roughly 5 to 11 years of age, kindergarten through fifth grade
examples: The article uses this framework to code the SEL program targets of the 11 reviewed interventions as cognitive, social, and emotional in table 1
key_sources: Stephanie M. Jones, Sophie P. Barnes, Rebecca Bailey, and Emily J. Doolittle. (2017). Promoting Social and Emotional Competencies in Elementary School. The Future of Children, Vol. 27, No. 1, Spring 2017. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1144815

article_title: Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course
citation: Murat Pasa Uysal. (2014). Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course. Contemporary Educational Technology, 5(3), 198-217. https://www.cedtech.net
title: Jonassen's Instructional Design Model for Well-Structured Problems (seven-step sequence)
description: The article adopts Jonassen's (1997) "Instructional Design Model for Well-Structured Problems" as the design theory for the experimental treatment. It prescribes a seven-step sequence: "Step-1: Presenting the problem", reviewing concepts, rules and principles, presenting conceptual models of the CP domain, presenting worked examples, presenting practice problems, supporting the search for different solutions, and reflecting on problem states and solutions. In the study the first four steps ran in lectures and the next three in lab hours, modeling CP as a well-structured PS process.
requirements: Well-defined programming problems with preferred or prescribed solutions, since well-structured problems "require application of finite number of rules, principles and concepts"
Instructor training in conducting PS-based course activities
constraints: The study applied the model only to well-structured problems; "the problems used in this study did not include ill-structured problems"
examples: Lectures started with a well-structured programming problem; flowcharts and pseudo codes formed conceptual models; worked examples used different loop types for the repetition-structures topic
key_sources: Murat Pasa Uysal. (2014). Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course. Contemporary Educational Technology, 5(3), 198-217. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105559

article_title: The Significance of Journal Writing in Improving Listening and Reading Comprehension in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA)
citation: Ina Saad, Magdi Ahmed. (2015). The Significance of Journal Writing in Improving Listening and Reading Comprehension in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11): 815-821. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031106
title: The journal learning continuum: topic selection, research, reflection, writing, coded feedback, self-correction and peer sharing
description: The article describes journal writing as "a learning continuum in which students have several opportunities to learn throughout the continuum chain." The cycle starts with selecting a journal scenario or topic with instructions and criteria; students research the topic, review relevant vocabulary, grammar or culture, reflect, and express an opinion in writing; teachers give feedback via correction codes; students find and correct their own errors, verify the corrections, and often share what they learned with fellow students. Assignments progressed from lower-order thinking tasks early in the course to higher-order thinking and problem-solving tasks in semester three.
requirements: Assignments need their own instructions and objectives, with criteria and measurable objectives set for journal writing
Students set a time limit for journal writing (40-60 minutes)
Journals are collected daily and feedback is given in the form of correction codes
constraints: The pattern was implemented within a fifty-week intensive government language course and the authors note the study is based on generalized knowledge that may or may not work for other similar classes
target_learners: adult foreign-language learners in an intensive MSA course, aged 29-35, with university education
target_learning_goals: listening and reading comprehension in Modern Standard Arabic
reflective and critical thinking in the target language
examples: One day a week students listened to news articles about a target-language country and wrote a comprehensive summary, relaying Essential Elements of Information and injecting personal opinions; in semester three this became twice weekly with critical thinking tasks
key_sources: Ina Saad, Magdi Ahmed. (2015). The Significance of Journal Writing in Improving Listening and Reading Comprehension in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11): 815-821. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031106

article_title: Explicit versus Implicit Modes of EFL Reading Literacy Instruction: Using Phonological Awareness with Adult Arab Learners
citation: Mahmoud Ibrahim. (2018). Explicit Versus Implicit Modes of EFL Reading Literacy Instruction: Using Phonological Awareness With Adult Arab Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p144
title: Jolly Phonics materials for adult EFL literacy intervention
description: Jolly Phonics is a freely available course book with audios and supplementary material, originally "primarily designed for very young learners", used here as the treatment medium over 24 one-hour sessions. It targets five skills: letter sounds and digraphs, letter forms, blends, segmentation, and tricky words with irregular spelling. Sounds were taught in a non-alphabetical order so learners could combine sounds into words earlier.
requirements: Audio recordings accompanying the material so students hear native production of the target sounds
Teachers who emphasize letter-sound associations rather than letter names
constraints: The article notes most available market material of this kind is designed for very young learners, prompting a recommendation that universities develop age-appropriate materials
target_learners: Adult Arab EFL foundation-year university students lacking basic English word-identification literacy
target_learning_goals: Decoding written English words aloud (word identification / reading literacy)
examples: Treatment lessons revised prior input, introduced new sounds with orthographic shapes and mnemonic imagery (e.g., the snake hissing sound /s/), then practiced blending and segmentation, ending with vocabulary memorization
key_sources: Mahmoud Ibrahim. (2018). Explicit Versus Implicit Modes of EFL Reading Literacy Instruction: Using Phonological Awareness With Adult Arab Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p144

article_title: Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course
citation: Liju Xu. (2018). Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course. English Language Teaching, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n10p145
title: Journal entry practice vocabulary enhancement activity
description: A vocabulary enhancement activity in which students in groups of three studied sets of business transactions with the number varying from 10 to 15, working out accounting terminologies and explaining the accounting treatment and principle in English, followed by an oral report. The activity was designed to reinforce the learning of accounting concepts and terminologies, which the authors link to better post-test outcomes than general exercises. By participating, students focused on special terms and learned their meanings and functions.
requirements: Activities must be designed around the characteristics of the ESP course and learners' subject matter knowledge level
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experimental study with accounting juniors at a single Chinese university
target_learning_goals: using terms accurately in professional tasks
examples: Group B students worked in groups of three on sets of 10-15 business transactions for 15-20 minutes, then gave oral reports
key_sources: Liju Xu. (2018). Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course. English Language Teaching, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n10p145

article_title: A Novel Student Engagement Analysis of Real Classroom Teaching Using Unified Body Orientation Estimation.
citation: Chen Yuqing, Li Jiawen, Liu Yixin, Jiang Fei. (2025). A Novel Student Engagement Analysis of Real Classroom Teaching Using Unified Body Orientation Estimation. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s25206421
title: JointBDOE one-stage unified body detection and orientation estimation model
description: JointBDOE is a single-stage, end-to-end trainable framework built on YOLOv11 that "integrates human bounding box prediction and body orientation into a unified embedding space, enabling the simultaneous and precise estimation of human positions and orientations in multi-person scenarios". It uses a CSPDarknet53 backbone, PANet neck, a decoupled three-branch head (classification, localization, orientation), a wrapped MSE loss for angle periodicity, and a probability-threshold filter for unreliable orientation estimates.
requirements: Training with reconstructed MEBOW annotations and pseudo-orientation labels; hyperparameters τ and λ tuned via ablation
constraints: Orientation is difficult to determine for severely occluded, highly truncated, or extremely small human instances
target_learners: Students in kindergarten through university classrooms
target_learning_goals: Non-intrusive detection of student engagement via body orientation in authentic classrooms
examples: Applied to classroom videos with row–column, group-discussion, teacher–student interaction, and circular seating arrangements
key_sources: Chen Yuqing, Li Jiawen, Liu Yixin, Jiang Fei. (2025). A Novel Student Engagement Analysis of Real Classroom Teaching Using Unified Body Orientation Estimation. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s25206421

article_title: Physical, mental and behavioral health indicators in relation to academic performance in European boys and girls: the I.Family study.
citation: Lin Qinyun, Hunsberger Monica, Klingberg Sofia, de Henauw Stefaan, Hebestreit Antje, Lauria Fabio, Mazur Artur, Moreno Luis, Noémi Kurdiné Molnár Eszter, Pigeot Iris, Tornaritis Michael, Veidebaum Toomas, Lissner Lauren. (2025). Physical, mental and behavioral health indicators in relation to academic performance in European boys and girls: the I.Family study. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-23578-3
title: Joint-effects conceptual model: physical, mental, behavioral, and sleep-related health indicators jointly influence academic performance
description: The article proposes that academic performance is shaped by the joint effects of health dimensions spanning physical, mental, behavioral, and sleep domains. Its conceptualization states that "behavioral factors such as media use and physical activity may impact academic performance directly or indirectly through physical and mental health indicators," for example physical activity improving fitness, well-being, or sleep quality. Eight indicators were selected across these domains (KINDL HRQoL, stressful life events, BMI, sleep duration and quality, healthy diet score, media use, sports club participation) and tested with multivariable regression conditional on the others. Sleep is treated as a separate domain due to its dual physical and behavioral role.
requirements: Data on multiple health domains measured in the same adolescents so each indicator's contribution can be assessed conditional on the others
Sex-stratified and subject-stratified analyses to capture heterogeneity in how indicators relate to mathematics and language
constraints: The article uses multivariable regression rather than modeling complex interdependencies such as through path analysis; associations are cross-sectional and not causal
target_learners: Adolescents aged 12 to 16.9 years in European school systems
target_learning_goals: Academic performance in mathematics and language subjects
examples: The I.Family analysis included eight health indicators identified from physical, mental, behavioral, and sleep-related aspects of adolescent health, adjusted for parents' education, income, age, and country fixed effects
key_sources: Lin Qinyun, Hunsberger Monica, Klingberg Sofia, de Henauw Stefaan, Hebestreit Antje, Lauria Fabio, Mazur Artur, Moreno Luis, Noémi Kurdiné Molnár Eszter, Pigeot Iris, Tornaritis Michael, Veidebaum Toomas, Lissner Lauren. (2025). Physical, mental and behavioral health indicators in relation to academic performance in European boys and girls: the I.Family study. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-23578-3

article_title: Trajectories of school absences across compulsory schooling and their impact on children's academic achievement: An analysis based on linked longitudinal survey and school administrative data.
citation: Dräger, J., Klein, M., & Sosu, E. M. (2024). Trajectories of school absences across compulsory schooling and their impact on children's academic achievement: An analysis based on linked longitudinal survey and school administrative data. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0306716
title: Joint authorised-unauthorised absence trajectory typology for compulsory schooling
description: The article proposes an organizing typology of absenteeism that models absences dynamically across the whole school career and jointly by reason. Using k-means clustering for longitudinal data, it distinguishes five patterns — from "Consistently Low Absences" through "Strongly Increasing Authorised Absences" — capturing the extent, timing, and variability of exposure to school-based learning. The typology underpins the argument that snapshot or single-year measures mask differences between students and underestimate absence effects.
requirements: Requires longitudinal absence data on both authorised and unauthorised absences across multiple school years (linked administrative records).
constraints: Derived from a pre-pandemic English cohort (born 2000/2001, school years 2006–2017); the authors note trajectories of post-pandemic cohorts may differ.
target_learners: Children in compulsory schooling (ages 5–16) in England
target_learning_goals: Maintaining school attendance to support cumulative academic achievement
examples: The study clustered years 1–11 joint absence data for 7,218 pupils into five named trajectory groups using the kml3d R package.
key_sources: Dräger, J., Klein, M., & Sosu, E. M. (2024). Trajectories of school absences across compulsory schooling and their impact on children's academic achievement: An analysis based on linked longitudinal survey and school administrative data. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0306716

article_title: Astronomy at school: present situation and future perspectives
citation: María Iglesias, Cynthia Quinteros y Alejandro Gangui. (2006). Astronomía en la escuela: situación actual y perspectivas futuras. CEFIEC-FCEyN-UBA. https://abc.gov.ar
title: Teacher educators and astronomers should attend to preservice teachers' alternative conceptions and work jointly, before pedagogical innovation is possible
description: The article argues that no pedagogical innovation in astronomy teaching is possible without first answering whether teachers understand the concepts they must teach: "ninguna innovación pedagógica será posible sin antes proveer un a adecuada respuesta a estos interrogantes". It recommends that teacher-educator institutes better prepare teachers in astronomy, that educators and astronomers "prestar especial atención a las concepciones "alternativas" de los futuros docentes", and that scientists and teacher educators collaborate and that such joint work be valued.
requirements: Willingness of scientists and teacher-educator institutions to collaborate and to value that joint work
constraints: The article offers this as a recommendation grounded in the reviewed literature, not as a tested intervention
target_learning_goals: accurate scientific understanding of basic astronomy content to be taught
examples: The article recommends workshop work, contrasting ideas and information, discovering inconsistencies and anomalies, building robust scientific knowledge and avoiding sedimentación de conocimientos
key_sources: María Iglesias, Cynthia Quinteros y Alejandro Gangui. (2006). Astronomía en la escuela: situación actual y perspectivas futuras. CEFIEC-FCEyN-UBA. https://abc.gov.ar
